Pones una sartén con agua sobre una plac: You put a pan of water on an induction hob and the water boils right away. But there is no flame or red-hot resistor: the glass underneath hardly heats up, and if you remove the pan, the hob is cold within a few seconds.\n\nSo how does it heat? It does not heat: **it makes the pan itself heat up**. The energy arrives without contact, through the magnetic field, and is turned into heat inside the metal of the base.

The electronics of the hob pass it an alternating current of about 25 kHz, and that current creates a magnetic field $B$ that crosses the glass and reaches the pan.\n\nAs the current changes direction 25,000 times per second, the field rises, falls and reverses at the same rate, $B(t) = B_0 "sin"(ω t)$. In the animation it is in slow motion, so you can see it.

La base de la sartén es un metal que el:
The base of the pan is a metal that the field passes through. Its flux is $Φ = B S$, and as $B$ changes, so does the flux. It is exactly what Faraday's law needs to induce an emf:

$ε = −{dΦ}/{dt} = −B_0 S ω cos(ω t)$

With $B_0$ = 3 mT, a base of 8 cm radius ($S$ = ${n(S * 1e4, 0)} cm²) and $ω = 2π · 25000 = ${miles(W)}$ rad/s, the maximum emf is $ε_0 = B_0 S ω$ = **${n(epsPico, 2)} V** (${n(epsEf, 2)} V rms). No wire is even needed: the field itself induces it.

Una fem en un metal macizo hace circular: An emf in a solid metal makes a current circulate: $I = ε / R$. In the base of the pan, which is a conductor with no wires, closed swirls of current form, the eddy currents (or parasitic currents).\n\nIf the base is modelled as an iron ring of 2 mm × 1 mm cross-section, its resistance is $R = ρ L/A = 10^{−7} · 0.503 / (2·10^{−6}) = ${n(R * 1e3, 1)} "mΩ"$, and the peak current, $I_0 = ε_0 / R$ = **${miles(Ipico)} A**. By Lenz's law, the current opposes the change in flux: it goes in the opposite direction to the one that would make the field grow.
de potencia con 25 kHz, como un fogón po: of power at 25 kHz, like a powerful hob; with the 50 Hz mains it would be only ${n(datos.P50 * 1e3, 1)} mW.
Una corriente que pasa por una resistenc: A current passing through a resistance heats it, this is the Joule effect: $P = {ε_"rms"^2}/R = {${n(epsEf, 2)}^2}/{${n(R, 4)}} = ${miles(P)} "W"$. It is the power of a cooker hob, and it comes from the metal itself, without passing through the glass.\n\nThe emf is proportional to the frequency, so the power is to $f^2$: with the 50 Hz mains we would get ${n(datos.P50 * 1e3, 1)} mW, nothing. That is why the hob works at tens of kHz. And that is why the pan must be iron: it is magnetic (it concentrates the field) and a poor conductor compared with copper. An aluminium or copper one hardly heats up, and the hob does not even detect it.
Foucault comprobó que un disco de cobre: Foucault found that a copper disc spinning between the poles of a magnet slows down and heats up.
Las mismas corrientes de Foucault tienen: The same eddy currents have another very visible effect. Drop a neodymium magnet down a plastic tube: it falls in a fraction of a second, like any stone (50 cm in about 0.32 s). Drop it down a copper tube of the same size and it takes several seconds.\n\nThe moving magnet changes the flux through each ring of the tube, and by Faraday a current is induced. By Lenz, that current creates a field that opposes the motion of the magnet and slows it down. The tube does not move, and the magnet touches nothing: the energy of the fall goes into heating the copper. The magnetic brakes of trains and roller coasters work this way.
